592.body:
Two datetimes are equal when they are the same instant, whatever their offsets (12:00Z equals 14:00+02:00). This is PostgreSQL's equality and TinkerPop's ("dates are evaluated based on the numerical comparison of Unix Epoch time"). The offset is kept and shown, but never compared: datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z") == datetime("2023-08-02T14:00+02:00") // true
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z"), datetime("2023-08-02T14:00+02:00")).dedup().count().next() // 1
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T14:00+02:00")).is(P.gt(datetime("2023-08-02T11:00Z"))).count().next() // 1 Of two values with the same instant and different offsets the first one met is kept (dedup(), a group() key); their order in a sort is unspecified. To compare the wall clocks instead, convert first: as_local() gives the wall-clock localdatetime ( Time Zones ).
592.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Comparing and Sorting » datetime: by its instant
592.title: datetime: by its instant

593.body:
Two durations are equal when their months, days and microseconds are equal: P1M is not P30D, and P1D is not PT24H (a day in a time zone may have 23 or 25 hours). Sorting compares their length as PostgreSQL does for an interval, counting a month as 30 days and a day as 24 hours; equal lengths are ordered by months, then days, then microseconds: duration("P1M") == duration("P30D") // false
g.inject(duration("P1M"), duration("P30D"), duration("PT719H")).order().to_list() // [PT719H, P30D, P1M]
593.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Comparing and Sorting » duration: field-wise equal, ordered by length
593.title: duration: field-wise equal, ordered by length

594.body:
A date, a localdatetime and a time compare by their calendar or clock value. g.inject(time("10:00")).is(P.between(time("09:00"), time("17:00"))).count().next() // 1
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).is(P.within(date("2023-08-02"), date("2023-08-03"))).count().next() // 1
594.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Comparing and Sorting » The other types: by calendar and clock
594.title: The other types: by calendar and clock

595.body:
Values of different types are never equal, and an ordering predicate between them does not match (no error): a date is not a datetime, and a date is never equal to a string, as a UUID is not. Convert one side first ( Conversions ). g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).is(P.eq("2023-08-02")).count().next() // 0
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).is(P.lt(datetime("2024-01-01T00:00Z"))).count().next() // 0
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).as_date().is(P.lt(datetime("2024-01-01T00:00Z"))).count().next() // 1 order() of a mixed stream puts the dates after the numbers and before the strings (TinkerPop's orderability places its date type there), in the order date, localdatetime, datetime, time, duration: g.inject("x", 1, duration("P1D"), time("01:00"), datetime("2023-08-02T00:00Z"), date("2023-08-02")).order().to_list()
595.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Comparing and Sorting » Different types
595.title: Different types

596.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Comparing and Sorting » Property indexes
596.title: Property indexes

597.body: Dates are read and written as ISO 8601 text (RFC 3339 for a datetime, with the RFC 9557 zone suffix). No locale formats, no two-digit years, no guessing: a text is read as a date only where a date is asked for (a constructor, a conversion step, a declared schema format, a typed value in a file).
597.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Text Formats » Text Formats
597.title: Text Formats

598.body:
Every value has one text, the one tables, JSON, GraphML, GraphSON and as_string() write. It is the text java.time writes, so other tools read it back: Type Canonical text date 2023-08-02; a year before 1 or after 9999 with its sign: -0044-03-15 time 09:30:00; a fraction only when it is not zero, as milliseconds or microseconds: 09:30:00.500, 09:30:00.123456 localdatetime 2023-08-02T09:30:00 (the date, T, the time) datetime 2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00; Z for a zero offset; an offset with seconds as +00:19:32 duration P1Y2M3DT4H5M6S: years and months from the months, days, then the time part; a zero part is left out, a zero duration is PT0S; a sign before P when every part is negative (-P1M2D), else a sign per part (P1M-2D) time("09:30:00.1").as_string() // "09:30:00.100"
datetime("2023-08-02 09:30+00:00").as_string() // "2023-08-02T09:30:00Z"
duration("PT90M").as_string() // "PT1H30M"
duration("P2W").as_string() // "P14D" A duration keeps its three fields as they are: PT36H stays PT36H (not P1DT12H), and weeks are read as 7 days. Years and months are one field, months: P1Y2M is 14 months.
598.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Text Formats » Canonical output
598.title: Canonical output

599.body:
Type Accepted text date YYYY-MM-DD; a year before 1 with its sign (-0044-03-15) time HH:MM, HH:MM:SS, HH:MM:SS.f with 1 to 9 fraction digits (digits below the microsecond are cut off) localdatetime a date, optionally followed by T (or t, or a space) and a time; a date alone is midnight datetime a local date-time, then an offset (Z, +02:00, +0200, +02, +00:19:32) and/or a zone in brackets ([Europe/Berlin]) duration [+-]P[nY][nM][nW][nD][T[nH][nM][n[.f]S]], a sign per number allowed (P1M-2D), letters in either case datetime("2023-08-02T09:30+0200") // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00")
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30[Europe/Berlin]") // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00")
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00.123456789Z") // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00.123456Z")
date("10000-01-01") // error: expected a four-digit year
duration("1 day") // error: not an ISO 8601 duration A datetime with only a zone is resolved in it (a wall-clock time the zone skips moves forward, one it repeats takes the earlier offset, see Time Zones ); with an offset and a zone the offset must be the zone's at that instant.
599.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Text Formats » What is read
599.title: What is read

rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown # one-time

python3 playground/serve.py 8000 # open http://localhost:8000/ The start page offers sample graphs, or a GraphSON or GraphML file of your own: The start page: choose a sample graph or load a file Pick Modern (TinkerPop) : four people, two pieces of software, and who knows and created what. Most examples in this book run on it.

60.body: g is the graph. v() starts one traverser on every vertex, has_label and has keep the ones that match, values turns each into a property value: g.v().has_label("person").values("name") // marko, vadas, josh, peter g.v().has_label("person").has("age", P.gt(30)).values("name") // josh, peter out(label) walks along outgoing edges, in(label) along incoming ones, both(label) along either: g.v().has("name", "marko").out("knows").values("name") // josh, vadas g.v().has("name", "marko").out("knows").out("created").values("name") // ripple, lop Edges are elements too: out_e steps onto the edges, in_v to their far end, and an edge can be filtered by its properties on the way: g.v().has_label("person").out_e("created").has("weight", P.gte(0.5)).in_v().values("name") // ripple
60.breadcrumbs: Gremlin in Ten Minutes » Start, filter, walk
60.title: Start, filter, walk

600.body:
TinkerPop reads a date-time text without an offset as UTC (asDate("2023-08-02") is midnight UTC). Graphersal does that only where a query asks for a conversion: lenient (no offset = UTC, a date alone = midnight UTC): the datetime() / DateTime() constructor and the conversion steps as_date() and as_date(GType.DATETIME); strict (an offset or a zone is required): every place a text is stored as a datetime, namely a property declared "format": "date-time" in the schema , the formatMinimum/formatMaximum bounds, a typed gx:OffsetDateTime in GraphSON or a change set, a saved query argument declared as a date-time, and the playground's property editor. datetime("2023-08-02T09:30") // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00Z")
g.inject("2023-08-02").as_date().next() // datetime("2023-08-02T00:00:00Z") A stored instant without its offset would be a guess about where it was written; the strict rule turns that guess into an error that names the expected form. The other types have no offset, so they read the same everywhere.
600.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Text Formats » Strict and lenient: a datetime without an offset
600.title: Strict and lenient: a datetime without an offset

601.body: A time zone is never stored in a value. A datetime carries a fixed UTC offset (the one it was written with); an operation that needs a zone takes it as an argument and gives back a datetime with the zone's offset at that instant. This is the PostgreSQL model (AT TIME ZONE, a session zone for the calendar arithmetic), with the zone passed explicitly instead of a session setting.
601.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Time Zones » Time Zones
601.title: Time Zones

602.body: A zone argument is one of: an IANA zone name : "Europe/Berlin", "America/New_York", "UTC"; a fixed offset : "+02:00", "-0530", "Z". The IANA rules come from the time zone database bundled with Graphersal (the jiff-tzdb crate). Every machine, and the browser playground, gives the same answer to the same query, and a replayed journal computes what it computed when it was written; the database changes only with a Graphersal release, not with an operating system update. An unknown name is an error, found before any value is read: g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).at_zone("Mars/Olympus").next() // error: unknown time zone The steps that take a zone: at_zone(zone) , as_local(zone) , date_add(.., zone) , date_diff(.., zone) , age(.., zone) , date_trunc(.., zone) , date_part(.., zone) , and today(zone). Only a datetime (and the localdatetime of at_zone) takes one; the other types have no instant, and a zone argument for them is an error.
602.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Time Zones » Zone arguments
602.title: Zone arguments

603.body:
at_zone(zone) on a datetime: the same instant, written with the zone's offset at it (PostgreSQL AT TIME ZONE, java.time atZoneSameInstant). at_zone(zone) on a localdatetime: the wall-clock time read in the zone, the datetime of that instant (java.time atZone). as_local() / as_local(zone): the wall-clock localdatetime a datetime shows on its own offset or in the zone (toLocalDateTime). g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).at_zone("America/New_York").next() // datetime("2023-08-02T08:00:00-04:00")
g.inject(localdatetime("2023-08-02T12:00")).at_zone("+02:00").next() // datetime("2023-08-02T12:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).as_local("Asia/Tokyo").next() // localdatetime("2023-08-02T21:00:00")
603.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Time Zones » Moving between a datetime and its wall clock
603.title: Moving between a datetime and its wall clock

604.body:
Where a zone moves its clocks, a wall-clock time can be missing (a spring-forward gap ) or happen twice (a fall-back fold ). Graphersal resolves both as PostgreSQL and java.time do (the "compatible" rule), never with an error: a time in a gap moves forward by the length of the gap: 02:30 on 2023-03-26 in Berlin becomes 03:30+02:00; a time in a fold takes the earlier offset: 02:30 on 2023-10-29 in Berlin is 02:30+02:00, the first of the two. g.inject(localdatetime("2023-03-26T02:30")).at_zone("Europe/Berlin").next() // datetime("2023-03-26T03:30:00+02:00")
g.inject(localdatetime("2023-10-29T02:30")).at_zone("Europe/Berlin").next() // datetime("2023-10-29T02:30:00+02:00") The same rule applies to a text with only a zone (datetime("2023-03-26T02:30[Europe/Berlin]")) and to every result a zone computes on the wall clock.
604.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Time Zones » Daylight saving: gaps and folds
604.title: Daylight saving: gaps and folds

605.body:
Without a zone a datetime is computed on its own fixed offset: date_add(DT.day, 1) adds 24 hours, as TinkerPop specifies. With a zone, calendar units work on the zone's wall clock, so a day stays a calendar day across a daylight saving change (23 or 25 hours long), while hours stay hours: g.inject(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00")).date_add(DT.day, 1).next() // datetime("2023-03-26T12:00:00+01:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00")).date_add(DT.day, 1, "Europe/Berlin").next() // datetime("2023-03-26T12:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00")).date_add(DT.hour, 24, "Europe/Berlin").next() // datetime("2023-03-26T13:00:00+02:00") The same holds for date_diff() in days and larger units, age(), date_trunc() and date_part(): they read the wall clock of the zone. Without a zone, date_diff() and age() read both operands on the wall clock of the second operand's offset: g.inject(datetime("2023-03-26T12:00+02:00")).date_diff(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00"), DT.day).next() // 0 (23 hours)
g.inject(datetime("2023-03-26T12:00+02:00")).date_diff(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00"), DT.day, "Europe/Berlin").next() // 1
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_trunc(DT.day, "America/New_York").next() // datetime("2023-08-02T00:00:00-04:00")
605.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Time Zones » Calendar arithmetic in a zone
605.title: Calendar arithmetic in a zone

606.body: Three steps compute with dates: date_add() moves a value, date_diff() measures the distance between two values as a number, age() as a duration. All of them are checked: a result outside the years -9999 to 9999 is an error, never a wrapped value. In a script the operators + and - do the same ( script values ).
606.title: Arithmetic

607.body: DT.second, DT.minute, DT.hour and DT.day are TinkerPop's (the bare names second, minute, hour and day work too, as in the TinkerPop scenarios). Graphersal adds the smaller and the calendar units, with PostgreSQL's field names: Unit Kind Adding it DT.microsecond, DT.millisecond, DT.second, DT.minute, DT.hour a fixed length moves the instant (or the clock) by that many microseconds DT.day, DT.week calendar days moves the wall-clock date; in a zone the time of day is kept across a daylight saving change DT.month, DT.quarter, DT.year, DT.decade, DT.century, DT.millennium calendar months (1, 3, 12, 120, 1200, 12000) moves the month and clamps the day to the end of the target month DT.day_of_week, DT.iso_day_of_week, DT.day_of_year, DT.iso_year, DT.epoch and DT.offset are parts, not units: only date_part() takes them.
607.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Arithmetic » Units: the DT token
607.title: Units: the DT token

608.body:
date_add(DT.unit, n) adds n units (a negative n subtracts); date_add(duration) adds a duration. Both take an optional zone as the last argument ( Time Zones ). g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_add(DT.hour, 36).next() // datetime("2023-08-04T00:00:00Z")
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).date_add(day, 3).next() // date("2023-08-05")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_add(DT.millisecond, 1500).next() // datetime("2023-08-02T12:00:01.500Z") Month ends. Adding months keeps the day of the month where it exists and otherwise takes the last day of the target month, as PostgreSQL and java.time do. Each step clamps on its own, so two single months can end earlier than two months at once: g.inject(date("2024-01-31")).date_add(DT.month, 1).next() // date("2024-02-29")
g.inject(date("2024-01-31")).date_add(DT.month, 2).next() // date("2024-03-31")
g.inject(date("2024-01-31")).date_add(DT.month, 1).date_add(DT.month, 1).next() // date("2024-03-29") A duration is added in PostgreSQL's order: its months first (clamped), then its days, then its time part. g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_add(duration("P1M1DT1H")).next() // datetime("2023-09-03T13:00:00Z")
g.inject(date("2024-02-29")).date_add(duration("P1Y1D")).next() // date("2025-03-01") What each type accepts: Type DT units A duration datetime all units; a fixed length moves the instant and keeps the offset (TinkerPop: a day is 24 hours at a fixed offset), with a zone the result takes the zone's offset any localdatetime all units, on the wall clock any date day and larger without a time part time hour and smaller; the clock wraps around midnight (PostgreSQL time + interval) without months or days duration all units: adds to the matching field any (field by field) g.inject(time("23:00")).date_add(DT.hour, 2).next() // time("01:00:00")
g.inject(date("2024-02-29")).date_add(DT.hour, 2).next() // error: adding the unit hour is not defined for a date
608.title: date_add()

609.body:
date_diff(other) is TinkerPop's dateDiff(): the incoming value minus other in milliseconds , an int64, each operand's epoch milliseconds rounded down. other is a value or a child traversal whose first result is the operand; () (null) stands for the epoch. g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_diff(datetime("2023-08-01T00:00Z")).next() // 129600000
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_diff(__.constant(datetime("2023-08-01T00:00Z"))).next() // 129600000
g.inject(datetime("1970-01-01T00:00:01Z")).date_diff(()).next() // 1000 Graphersal extends it to the other types (both operands of one type: a date counts from midnight, a time within the day; () is 1970-01-01 or midnight) and adds date_diff(other, DT.unit[, zone]): the difference in whole units , truncated toward zero. Units below a day count the elapsed time. Days and weeks count wall-clock days (a datetime on the wall clock of other's offset, or of the zone). Months and larger count as java.time's ChronoUnit.between: a month is complete when the day of the month (and the time) is reached again, so January 31 to February 28 is 0 months. g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_diff(datetime("2023-08-01T00:00Z"), DT.hour).next() // 36
g.inject(time("10:00")).date_diff(time("09:00"), DT.minute).next() // 60
g.inject(date("2024-02-28")).date_diff(date("2024-01-31"), DT.month).next() // 0
g.inject(date("2024-03-31")).date_diff(date("2024-02-29"), DT.month).next() // 1
609.title: date_diff()

61.breadcrumbs: Gremlin in Ten Minutes » Remember and come back
61.title: Remember and come back

610.body:
age(other[, zone]) is PostgreSQL's age: the difference as a duration of whole years and months, days and a time part, all with the same sign. It is counted down from the incoming value to other with PostgreSQL's borrowing rules, so swapping the operands negates the result. Both operands have the same type; () is an error. g.inject(date("2001-04-10")).age(date("1957-06-13")).next() // duration("P43Y9M27D")
g.inject(date("1957-06-13")).age(date("2001-04-10")).next() // duration("-P43Y9M27D")
g.inject(datetime("2024-02-29T00:00Z")).age(datetime("2023-01-31T12:00Z")).next() // duration("P1Y28DT12H") To get a plain number of days, years or hours, use date_diff(other, DT.unit); to get a duration of elapsed time without calendar units, subtract the two values in a script (a - b).
610.title: age()

611.body: date_trunc(DT.unit) is PostgreSQL's date_trunc, and date_part(DT.unit) is its extract. Both are Graphersal extensions; TinkerPop has neither. A datetime is read on its own wall clock, or on the wall clock of a zone given as the last argument ( Time Zones ).
611.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Truncation and Parts » Truncation and Parts
611.title: Truncation and Parts

612.body:
The fields below the unit become their first value: the start of the hour, the day, the month. A truncated datetime keeps its offset (or, with a zone, takes the zone's offset at the new instant). g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_trunc(DT.hour).next() // datetime("2023-08-17T15:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_trunc(DT.week).next() // datetime("2023-08-14T00:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_trunc(DT.day, "UTC").next() // datetime("2023-08-17T00:00:00Z")
g.inject(date("2023-08-17")).date_trunc(DT.quarter).next() // date("2023-07-01")
g.inject(duration("P1Y2M3DT4H5M")).date_trunc(DT.day).next() // duration("P1Y2M3D") Unit Truncates to microsecond ... hour the start of that unit of the clock day midnight week Monday, midnight (ISO 8601 weeks) month, quarter, year the first day of the month, of the quarter (January, April, July, October), of the year decade the first day of a year divisible by 10 (2020-01-01) century, millennium the first day of a year ending in 01/001: centuries and millennia start at year 1, as PostgreSQL counts them (2001-01-01 starts the 21st century) A date takes day and larger, a time hour and smaller, a duration keeps the fields at and above the unit (month and larger keep whole multiples of the unit's months and drop the days and the time part).
612.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Truncation and Parts » date_trunc()
612.title: date_trunc()

613.body:
One field as a number: an int64, except DT.epoch, a float64 of seconds. Part Value DT.year, DT.month (1-12), DT.day (1-31), DT.hour, DT.minute, DT.second (0-59) the field DT.millisecond (0-999), DT.microsecond (0-999999) the fraction of the second; unlike PostgreSQL, not the seconds with the fraction DT.quarter (1-4) the quarter DT.week (1-53) the ISO 8601 week number DT.iso_year the ISO 8601 week-numbering year (2023-01-01 is in week 52 of 2022) DT.day_of_week 0 = Sunday to 6 = Saturday (PostgreSQL dow) DT.iso_day_of_week 1 = Monday to 7 = Sunday (PostgreSQL isodow) DT.day_of_year (1-366) the day of the year DT.decade, DT.century, DT.millennium as PostgreSQL counts them (the 21st century is 2001-2100) DT.epoch seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z (a localdatetime read as UTC); for a duration its length with a year of 365.25 days and a month of 30 days DT.offset the UTC offset of a datetime in seconds g.inject(date("2023-08-17")).date_part(DT.day_of_week).next() // 4
g.inject(datetime("2023-01-01T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.week).next() // 52
g.inject(datetime("2023-01-01T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.iso_year).next() // 2022
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.epoch).next() // 1692280032.5
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.offset).next() // 7200
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T02:00Z")).date_part(DT.day, "America/New_York").next() // 1 A date has no clock parts (hour and smaller), a time only those (and epoch, the seconds since midnight). A duration gives PostgreSQL's interval fields: year and month from its months (14 months are 1 year and 2 months), day its days, hour and smaller from its time part; it has no week, day-of parts, iso_year or offset: g.inject(duration("P1Y2M3DT4H5M6.5S")).date_part(DT.month).next() // 2
g.inject(date("2023-08-17")).date_part(DT.hour).next() // error: the part hour is not defined for a date
613.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Truncation and Parts » date_part()
613.title: date_part()

614.body: A value becomes a date only through an explicit step; nothing is converted by guessing (a string that looks like a date stays a string).
614.title: Conversions

615.body:
as_date() converts to a datetime exactly as TinkerPop's asDate() does: Incoming Result a datetime unchanged a string read leniently as ISO 8601 / RFC 3339: without an offset it is UTC, a date alone is midnight UTC ( Text Formats ) an int64 milliseconds since the epoch, in UTC a date, a localdatetime the datetime at UTC (Graphersal: TinkerPop has no such types) anything else (a float64, (), a list, a map, a time, a duration, an element) an error starting with "Can't parse", as in TinkerPop g.inject("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00", 1690000000000, date("2023-08-02")).as_date().to_list() // [2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00, 2023-07-22T04:26:40Z, 2023-08-02T00:00:00Z]
g.inject(1.5).as_date().next() // error: Can't parse float64 1.5 as a datetime
615.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Conversions » as_date(): TinkerPop's asDate()
615.title: as_date(): TinkerPop's asDate()

616.body:
as_date(GType.DATETIME | DATE | LOCALDATETIME | TIME) converts to that type (a Graphersal extension, spelled like as_number(GType.LONG)): Incoming → DATETIME DATE LOCALDATETIME TIME string lenient, as as_date() strict: a date text strict: a local date-time text strict: a time text datetime unchanged its wall-clock date (at its own offset) its wall clock its wall-clock time localdatetime at UTC its date unchanged its time date midnight UTC unchanged midnight an error time an error an error an error unchanged int64 epoch milliseconds, UTC an error an error an error GType.DURATION is not a target here: use as_duration(). To read a datetime's wall clock in another zone, use as_local(zone) first ( Time Zones ). g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T23:30-07:00")).as_date(GType.DATE).next() // date("2023-08-02")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T23:30-07:00")).as_local("UTC").as_date(GType.DATE).next() // date("2023-08-03")
g.inject("2023-08-02").as_date(GType.DATE).next() // date("2023-08-02")
g.inject("2023-08-02T09:30").as_date(GType.DATE).next() // error: unexpected text after the value
616.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Conversions » as_date(GType.X): to another date type
616.title: as_date(GType.X): to another date type

617.body: as_duration() reads an ISO 8601 duration text; a duration passes unchanged, anything else fails with "Can't parse". g.inject("PT90M").as_duration().next() // duration("PT1H30M")
617.title: as_duration()

618.body:
as_number() of a datetime is its epoch milliseconds (TinkerPop), rounded down; the other date types are not numbers (use date_part(DT.epoch) or date_diff()). as_string() of any date is its canonical text; in a script, x.as_string() does the same. cast(GType.DATETIME) (and the other date tokens) parses a string or, for DATETIME, reads an int64 as epoch milliseconds, like as_date(GType.X). g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T00:00Z")).as_number().next() // 1690934400000
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T09:30+02:00")).as_string().next() // "2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00"
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).as_number().next() // error: Cast exception
618.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Conversions » To numbers and text
618.title: To numbers and text

619.body: A property written as a string stays a string. To store dates, declare the property in the schema ("format": "date-time"): in open and closed mode a string written to it is converted on write. Or convert in the query: property("at", __.constant(text).as_date()), or write a date value (property("on", date("2023-08-02"))).

62.body:
Some steps need the whole stream before they answer: count, group, order, dedup. by(...) modulates the step before it, and __. starts an anonymous traversal that runs for each element: g.v().count() // 6 g.v().has_label("person").order().by("age", Order.desc).values("name") // peter, josh, marko, vadas g.v().has_label("person").group().by("name").by(__.out("created").count())
// {josh: 2, marko: 1, peter: 1, vadas: 0}
62.breadcrumbs: Gremlin in Ten Minutes » Group, count, order
62.title: Group, count, order

620.body:
now() is the current time as a datetime in UTC; today() is its date, and today(zone) the date in a zone (an IANA name or an offset). type_of(now()) // "datetime"
now() == now() // true
type_of(today("Europe/Berlin")) // "date"
g.add_v("event").property("at", now()).values("at").count().next() // 1
620.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » now() and today() » now() and today()
620.title: now() and today()

621.body:
Like PostgreSQL's now() (CURRENT_TIMESTAMP), now() is the time the script evaluation started , the same value for every call in it: a script that stamps a thousand elements stamps them all with one instant, and now() == now() holds. In the playground a whole script is one unit, so now() is the start of that unit. A saved query called from a script sees its caller's now(). now() and today() are script functions, evaluated before the traversal runs: the traversal gets the resulting value as a constant (inject(now()), property("at", now()), has("at", P.lt(now()))). The journal of a Store and a change set record that value, never the call, so a replay or a recovery writes the same instant, not the time of the replay. today() is the date of now() in UTC, PostgreSQL's current_date in a UTC session. For the date in another zone pass the zone, or convert the instant yourself: today("UTC") == today() // true
g.inject(now()).as_local("America/Los_Angeles").as_date(GType.DATE).next() == today("America/Los_Angeles") // true
621.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » now() and today() » The start of the evaluation
621.title: The start of the evaluation

622.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » now() and today() » Pinning the clock (hosts)
622.title: Pinning the clock (hosts)

623.body: A schema declares a date property as a JSON Schema string with a format, and bounds it with the format* keywords. The full reference (every keyword, the errors and why, inference and diffs) is on the Schemas page; this page is the overview. format Type Example value date-time datetime 2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00 local-date-time localdatetime 2024-05-01T09:30:00 (a Graphersal name: JSON Schema has none) date date 2024-05-01 time time 09:30:00 (local; JSON Schema's own time requires an offset) duration duration P1Y2M3DT4H JSON Schema validators treat format as an annotation and ignore one they do not know, so a schema with these formats stays usable with other tools; Pydantic writes date-time, date, time and duration for datetime, date, time and timedelta fields.
623.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Dates in a Schema » Dates in a Schema
623.title: Dates in a Schema

624.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Dates in a Schema » Coercion on write
624.title: Coercion on write

625.body:
formatMinimum, formatMaximum, formatExclusiveMinimum and formatExclusiveMaximum (the keywords of JSON Schema's format-comparison proposal, which ajv-formats implements) bound a date property. Their value is the text of a value of the node's type, and a value is compared as the type compares : a datetime by its instant, a duration by its length. minimum and maximum stay number keywords. { "type": "string", "format": "date-time", "formatMinimum": "2020-01-01T00:00:00Z" }
{ "type": "string", "format": "duration", "formatExclusiveMaximum": "P1D" }
625.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Dates in a Schema » Bounds
625.title: Bounds

626.body: infer_schema() reports a stored date with its format ({"type": "string", "format": "date-time"}), and a position that holds strings and dates as an anyOf, so freezing the structure you have (g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed)) keeps the dates dates. The playground's schema editor offers the five formats as types and their bounds as constraints.
626.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Dates in a Schema » Inference
626.title: Inference

627.body: A date keeps its type wherever it goes: in memory, in a snapshot or a Store, in a change set and in a GraphSON file. GraphML has no date type and needs the schema.
627.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Storage and Exchange » Storage and Exchange
627.title: Storage and Exchange

628.body: A date is stored inline in the property value, 16 bytes at most, without a heap allocation: a date is a day number, a time and a localdatetime microseconds, a datetime microseconds since the epoch plus its offset in seconds, a duration its months, days and microseconds. Equality and ordering compare these numbers ( Comparing and Sorting ).
628.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Storage and Exchange » In memory
628.title: In memory

629.body: The binary format (packed snapshots .gsnap, Store segments, the write-ahead log) has a value tag per type, 9 to 13, defined in the format specification : the exact payload, the range of each type, and the rule that a datetime keeps its offset while equality uses the instant. These tags came with file format version 2 : a build that knows them writes version 2 and reads versions 1 and 2, so a .gsnap written by 0.1.x still loads, while an older build refuses a version 2 file instead of misreading it. See Format Versions and Upgrade for a Store written by 0.1.x.
629.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Storage and Exchange » Snapshots, journals and the Store
629.title: Snapshots, journals and the Store

63.body:
repeat runs a traversal again and again, times(n) or until(condition) stops it, and emit() also yields the steps in between: // a path from peter to vadas, in either direction along the edges
g.v().has("name", "peter") .repeat(__.both().simple_path()).until(__.has("name", "vadas")) .path().by("name").limit(1) // [peter, lop, marko, vadas]
63.title: Loops

630.body: A serialized ChangeSet (feature serde) writes a date as a per-value type tag in TinkerPop's GraphSON style, so a replay restores the type without a schema: Type Tag datetime {"@type": "gx:OffsetDateTime", "@value": "2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00"} date, localdatetime, time gx:LocalDate, gx:LocalDateTime, gx:LocalTime duration of microseconds only gx:Duration (PT26H) duration of months and days only gx:Period (P1Y2M3D) any other duration graphersal:Interval (P1MT2H) Reading is strict: the text must be a value of the tag's type, and a gx:OffsetDateTime must carry its offset.
630.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Storage and Exchange » Change sets
630.title: Change sets

631.body: GraphSON 3.0 reads and writes the java.time types: g:Date/g:Timestamp (epoch milliseconds) become a datetime in UTC, gx:OffsetDateTime, gx:Instant and gx:ZonedDateTime a datetime with the offset of the text (the zone id of a gx:ZonedDateTime is dropped and reported), gx:LocalDate, gx:LocalDateTime and gx:LocalTime the local types, gx:Duration and gx:Period a duration. The export writes the tags of the change set table above, which TinkerGraph's g.io(file).read() loads, with one exception: a duration with both months or days and a time part has no java.time type, so it is written as graphersal:Interval, which only Graphersal reads (a deliberate deviation ). Digits below a microsecond are cut and reported, and the java.time types Graphersal cannot hold (gx:Year, gx:YearMonth, gx:MonthDay, gx:OffsetTime, gx:ZoneOffset) are skipped and reported. The full mapping is on the GraphSON page. A date-like string without a type tag (GraphSON 1.0, types=false) stays a string; declare the property in the schema to store it as a date.
631.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Storage and Exchange » GraphSON
631.title: GraphSON

632.body: GraphML has no date type: a date is written as its canonical text under a string key. It is read back as a date only when the target graph's schema declares the property with a date format: set the schema on the empty graph first, then import (the playground's "Load from file" takes the schema file next to the graph file; the CLI's --schema). Without a schema the text stays a string. See UUID Values , which describes the same rule for UUIDs, and the Schemas page.
632.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Storage and Exchange » GraphML
632.title: GraphML

633.body: Tables, JSON results, the CLI's visualizers, MCP and the dev server write the canonical text ("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00"); a script value prints as its literal (datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00")). The playground's property editor keeps the type: it shows and edits a date property as one of the five date types ( Text Formats ).
633.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » Storage and Exchange » JSON, tables and the playground
633.title: JSON, tables and the playground

634.body:
The Python binding converts the five types to and from the standard datetime module, both as results and as params=, to the microsecond (the resolution of both sides): Graphersal Python datetime aware datetime.datetime with tzinfo=datetime.timezone(timedelta(seconds=offset)) localdatetime naive datetime.datetime date datetime.date time naive datetime.time duration without months datetime.timedelta duration with months graphersal.Interval(months, days, micros) import datetime as dt
import graphersal graph = graphersal.Graph()
at = dt.datetime(2023, 8, 2, 9, 30, tzinfo=dt.timezone(dt.timedelta(hours=2)))
graph.query("g.inject(x).date_add(DT.day, 1).next()", params={"x": at})
# datetime.datetime(2023, 8, 3, 9, 30, tzinfo=datetime.timezone(datetime.timedelta(seconds=7200)))
graph.query('duration("P1Y2M")')
# Interval('P1Y2M') An aware datetime with any tzinfo (a zoneinfo.ZoneInfo too) is passed with the UTC offset it has at that instant; the zone name is not kept. An offset with a fraction of a second is refused. An aware datetime.time is refused: a time of day has no instant without a date. A timedelta becomes whole days and the rest, both with the sign of the whole (timedelta(hours=-1) is -PT1H). graphersal.Interval is immutable, equal when its three fields are equal (Interval("P1M") != Interval(0, 30), as in the engine), has months, days, micros and to_iso(), and is built from the fields or from ISO 8601 text (Interval("P1Y2M3DT4H")). Python's datetime holds the years 1 to 9999; a date before year 1 cannot be returned as one (read it with as_string()). The binding's README has the details and more examples.
634.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » From Python » From Python
634.title: From Python

635.body: TinkerPop 3.8 has one date type, datetime (a Java OffsetDateTime), the literal datetime(..), the steps asDate(), dateAdd() and dateDiff(), the units DT.second, DT.minute, DT.hour and DT.day, and the tokens GType.DATETIME and GType.DURATION (a Java Duration, which no TinkerPop step produces). Graphersal implements all of it as TinkerPop specifies, with no deviation: datetime("..") (also spelled DateTime("..")) reads ISO 8601 text, a text without an offset as UTC; asDate() converts text and epoch milliseconds, and fails with "Can't parse" for the same inputs as TinkerPop; dateAdd(DT.unit, n) keeps the offset and moves the instant, a day being 24 hours; dateDiff(other) is the difference in milliseconds, null being the epoch; asNumber() of a datetime is its epoch milliseconds; equality and ordering use the instant ("Dates are evaluated based on the numerical comparison of Unix Epoch time"), and dates sort after numbers and before strings. Every date scenario of the vendored TinkerPop 3.8.2 suite passes (DateTime, AsDate, DateAdd, DateDiff, the date cases of TypeOf and AsNumber), except two Orderability scenarios that also hold a set literal ({"x", "y", "z"}), for which Graphersal has no value type ( TinkerPop Compliance ).
635.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » TinkerPop Compatibility » TinkerPop Compatibility
635.title: TinkerPop Compatibility

636.body: Everything else on the pages of this part is a Graphersal extension, modelled on PostgreSQL: the types date, localdatetime and time (GType.DATE, LOCALDATETIME, TIME; typeOf names LocalDate, LocalDateTime, LocalTime), and duration as a value with months, days and microseconds (PostgreSQL's interval, broader than Java's Duration), with their constructors; the units DT.microsecond, DT.millisecond, DT.week to DT.millennium and the parts DT.day_of_week, DT.iso_day_of_week, DT.day_of_year, DT.iso_year, DT.epoch, DT.offset; date_add(duration), zone arguments, date_diff(other, DT.unit), age(), date_trunc(), date_part(), at_zone(), as_local(), as_duration(), as_date(GType.X); now(), today(), the getters and operators of script values; the schema formats and bounds, GraphSON's java.time types beyond g:Date, and the Python mapping . The extensions add behaviour where TinkerPop defines none; none of them changes what a TinkerPop step returns. The one deliberate difference in the exchange formats is GraphSON's graphersal:Interval for a duration that no java.time type can hold ( Storage and Exchange ); all deviations are listed on TinkerPop Deviations .
636.breadcrumbs: Dates and Times » TinkerPop Compatibility » Extensions
636.title: Extensions

637.body: A graph can store a schema: which vertex and edge labels exist, which properties they carry, of which types and within which constraints, and how edges may connect labels. The schema is plain data in one format, the same in Rust, the script DSL, Python and the playground: our envelope outside, standard JSON Schema 2020-12 inside (a strict subset), so a model_json_schema() from Pydantic can be pasted as a label's schema. The rule behind enforcement: the storage owns consistency. Every operation that changes the graph passes the schema inside one storage call, never in a step, and every traversal is one unit of work: it is applied completely or not at all.
637.title: Schemas

638.title: A first schema

639.body:
A common way to start: build the graph without a schema, experiment until the shape is right, then freeze that shape so every later write has to follow it: g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed) // or SchemaMode.open / SchemaMode.none set_schema(schema, mode) stores schema with its mode replaced by mode (an inferred schema has mode none, which enforces nothing). The mode is a SchemaMode token (SchemaMode.closed, SchemaMode::closed) or one of the strings "none", "open", "closed"; validate_schema(schema, mode) is the dry run. SchemaMode is a reserved name in the script scope. Binding Freeze DSL g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed) (also setSchema(.., "closed")) Rust let s = g.infer_schema()?.with_mode(SchemaMode::Closed); g_mut.set_schema(s)? Python graph.set_schema(graph.infer_schema(), mode="closed") Playground Schema panel: Freeze as open / Freeze as closed (shown while the graph stores no enforcing schema) What each mode freezes: open: the labels and properties that exist get their types and required lists; new labels and new properties stay allowed (unchecked). closed: additionally, no other label, no other property (at any depth) and no edge between other labels than the ones that exist. It always succeeds on the data the schema was inferred from , in both modes: inference declares every kind seen at every position and requires only the keys every element has (see Inference ). The one exception is closed with elements without a label : an unlabeled vertex or edge has no label to declare, and a closed schema admits only declared labels. Then the call fails, changes nothing, and the report names them: Cannot apply the Closed schema: the existing data violates it (2 kinds of violations on 2 elements of 6 checked) 1) 1 edge without a label (Closed admits only declared labels) [ids: "7"] 2) 1 vertex without a label (Closed admits only declared labels) [ids: "3"] Freeze such a graph in open mode (it admits unlabeled elements unchecked), or give those elements a label first with the label steps ( add_label, drop_label, set_label ) and freeze again: g.v("3").add_label("thing").to_list(); // a vertex from the report
g.e().not(__.has_label()).set_label("link").to_list(); // every unlabeled edge
g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed) (g.v().not(__.has_label()).add_label("thing") labels every unlabeled vertex; Rust: the same steps, or GraphStorage::add_vertex_label/set_edge_label.) (The generated large sample graph has unlabeled edges: it freezes open, not closed.) Later changes go through patch_schema (add a property, relax a rule) like any other schema.
639.breadcrumbs: Schemas » Freeze the structure you have
639.title: Freeze the structure you have

64.body:
A traversal without a final step is displayed (a table in the command line and the playground). In code, a terminal step returns the data: to_list() all results, next() the first one, iterate() runs it for its side effects only. let names = g.v().has_label("person").values("name").to_list(); // a list
let marko = g.v().has("name", "marko").next(); // one vertex
names.len() // 4
64.title: Results

641.body: Key Type Meaning $schema string, optional The format: https://graphersal.dev/schema/v1 (any other value is an error). meta object, optional Free-form data the library stores, round-trips and never interprets (a version, a status, server data). Changing it is a schema change. mode "none" | "open" | "closed", default "none" What is enforced, see Modes . vertices object Vertex label → {"schema": <label schema>}. edges object Edge label → {"connections": [{"from": .., "to": ..}], "schema": <label schema>}. A label schema is a JSON Schema object node describing the element's property map: {"type": "object", "properties": {..}, "required": [..], "additionalProperties": ..} plus annotations. It may carry $defs (for $ref), $schema and $id (accepted and not stored). A label without schema declares no properties. A connection's from/to is a vertex label or * (any label). Unknown keys are errors everywhere , the envelope included: {"mdoe": "closed"} is rejected with its location (Invalid schema at /mdoe: unknown key 'mdoe'), never silently ignored. The canonical form (what get_schema, to_json and every binding return) always writes $schema, mode, vertices and edges, keywords in a fixed order, integers as integers. The empty schema (mode none, no meta, no labels) is no schema: set_schema({}) removes the stored schema. The format is described by the meta-schema graphersal-schema-v1.json (graphersal::schema::META_SCHEMA_JSON).
641.title: Envelope

642.body: JSON Schema Engine type Note "integer" int64 A value outside i64 cannot be stored at all; 3.0 is not an integer. "number" float64 An int64 written to it is coerced when exactly representable; a stored int64 does not conform. "string" string "string" + "format": "uuid" uuid A canonical UUID string is coerced on write; a stored string does not conform. "string" + "format": "date-time" datetime An instant with its UTC offset (2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00). "string" + "format": "date" date A calendar day (2024-05-01). "string" + "format": "local-date-time" localdatetime A date and time without a zone (2024-05-01T09:30:00). A Graphersal format name: JSON Schema has none. "string" + "format": "time" time A time of day without an offset (09:30:00). JSON Schema's own time requires an offset; Graphersal's is local. "string" + "format": "duration" duration ISO 8601 (P1Y2M3DT4H): months, days and microseconds. "boolean", "null" boolean, null "array" + items array<T> items is a full schema (constraints and nullability apply to the items); without items any item. "array" + "format": "vector" (+ element, dimension, metric) vector<f32, 768> A vector of the declared element (f32 default, f16, i8, bit) and dimension (optional). A list of numbers is coerced on write, a vector of another element quantized; a stored list does not conform. items is not allowed next to it; metric is an annotation. Book page Vectors . "object" + properties object With required and additionalProperties. ["integer", "null"] union<int64|null> A type array: any of the listed types. anyOf: [..] union<..> At least one member accepts the value (Pydantic's Optional[X] is anyOf: [X, {"type": "null"}]). {} (no type) any Admits every value. Diagnostics, Display and GType keep the engine's names (int64, float64, uuid, datetime, localdatetime, ...). Dates and times. In open and closed mode a property declared with a temporal format coerces a string on write: any text the type's parser accepts (ISO 8601 / RFC 3339; the canonical form and the usual variants such as 2024-05-01 09:30Z or 09:30) becomes the temporal value, and text it refuses is a coercion failure that names the expected form. A date-time text must carry its UTC offset or a time zone (2024-05-01T09:30:00Z, 2024-05-01T09:30[Europe/Berlin]): 2024-05-01T09:30 is refused, never read as UTC, and the same holds for a formatMinimum/formatMaximum bound and a typed gx:OffsetDateTime (only the explicit conversion step as_date() keeps TinkerPop's "no offset is UTC"). This is the explicit declaration at work, like the uuid coercion, never a guess from content: an undeclared date-like string stays a string. A stored string does not conform to a temporal format (reads never coerce), and one temporal type never conforms to another (a date is not a datetime). JSON Schema's format is an annotation for other validators, which ignore a format they do not know, so a schema with local-date-time stays usable with them. The part Dates and Times describes the types themselves; its page Dates in a Schema has examples.
642.title: Types

643.body:
Kind Keywords Structure type, format (uuid, date-time, date, local-date-time, time, duration on a string; vector on an array), element, dimension, metric (with format: "vector"), items, properties, required, additionalProperties (true/false), anyOf Constraints minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum (numbers), formatMinimum, formatMaximum, formatExclusiveMinimum, formatExclusiveMaximum (dates and times), minLength, maxLength, pattern (strings), minItems, maxItems (arrays), enum, const (any value) Annotations (no effect on validation) title, description, $comment, examples, deprecated Create-time defaults ( Defaults on create ) default (also an annotation below the top level), defaultFunction (uuidv4, uuidv7, now, today) References $ref: "#/$defs/Name" with $defs at the label schema's root; inlined when the schema is loaded A constraint applies to the values of its own kind and ignores the others (JSON Schema semantics): in {"type": ["integer", "string"], "minimum": 10, "minLength": 3} the bound checks the integers and the length the strings. Next to a declared type, a keyword of another kind is an error (minLength on an integer is a mistake, not a no-op). enum/const compare JSON values (1 equals 1.0, a uuid and a date or time compare as their canonical text, so a datetime matches only the text with its own offset). formatMinimum, formatMaximum, formatExclusiveMinimum and formatExclusiveMaximum bound a date or time: the keywords of JSON Schema's format-comparison proposal (ajv-formats implements them; other validators ignore unknown keywords). Their value is the text of a value of the node's temporal format, and they are valid only next to one (minimum stays a number keyword): { "type": "string", "format": "date-time", "formatMinimum": "2020-01-01T00:00:00Z" }
{ "type": "string", "format": "duration", "formatExclusiveMaximum": "P1D" } A value is compared with its type's ordering: a datetime by its instant (2020-01-01T01:00:00+01:00 equals the minimum above), a duration by its length (a month counts 30 days, a day 24 hours, as PostgreSQL orders intervals), the others by their calendar or clock value. Local references are inlined : a loaded schema has no $ref/$defs, and a reference cycle is an error (recursive schemas are not supported). Only annotations, default and defaultFunction may sit next to a $ref; they override the definition's.
643.title: Keywords

644.body: Input Why it is rejected An unknown key or keyword, anywhere A typo must never weaken a schema silently. format other than uuid, date-time, date, local-date-time, time, duration (email, uri, ...) Accepting an unknown format as a plain string now would let a later version silently change what an existing schema accepts. Remove the format (the value is a string). formatMinimum (and the other format bounds) without a temporal format, or with text that is not of the format's type A bound needs the type it compares in; the hint shows an example of the type's text. additionalProperties: {schema} (a map of T, Pydantic dict[str, T]) No map type yet. Use {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": true}. oneOf, allOf, not, if/then/else Not implemented; anyOf covers oneOf when the members cannot both match. prefixItems, contains, tuples (items: [..]) An array has one item schema. uniqueItems, multipleOf Not yet (additive later). patternProperties, propertyNames, minProperties, dependent*, unevaluated* Keys are declared with properties, required, additionalProperties. readOnly, writeOnly, content* Not among the accepted annotations. A remote or non-$defs $ref, a reference cycle References are inlined at load. nullable, variants, min, min_length, int64, ... (spellings of other schema dialects, such as OpenAPI's nullable) The hint names the JSON Schema spelling. Every error is SchemaError::InvalidSchema { path, reason, hint }, path a JSON Pointer into the input (/vertices/person/schema/properties/age/minimum), and its help names the fix.
644.breadcrumbs: Schemas » What is an error, and why
644.title: What is an error, and why

645.title: Defaults on create

646.body: required (on the object) and nullability (the type) are independent, as in JSON Schema: null not admitted ("type": "string") null admitted ("type": ["string", "null"]) in required must be present, non-null must be present, may be null not in required may be absent, never null may be absent or null A missing required key is MissingRequiredProperty; a null where the type does not admit it is a TypeMismatch (expected string, got null). null stays a real stored value (property("k", ()) stores it, it never removes a property: use remove_property, see Removing Properties ). Inside a JSON value {"a": null} differs from {}. Required properties must be supplied when an element is created. The optimizer rule add_property_fold folds addV(..)/addE(..) and the property(k, v) steps that follow into one creation, so g.addV("Person").property("name", "Ann").property("age", 30) creates a valid element in one call. With the rule disabled, or for a property() that cannot be folded, the empty creation is rejected before anything is written. Removing a required property is rejected in open and closed mode.
646.title: Required and nullable

647.body: none open closed Coercion on write (canonical string to uuid, date and time text to its declared type, int64 to float64) no declared properties declared properties Types, constraints, required of declared labels (any depth) no yes yes Undeclared labels allowed allowed, unchecked rejected (also unlabeled elements) Default additionalProperties of an object node - true false Defaults on create (default, defaultFunction) no yes yes Edge topology (connections) no no yes mode governs undeclared labels and topology, and it is the default additionalProperties of every node typed object that does not state its own. An explicit value wins, both ways: a free-form object in a closed graph is {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": true}, a strict object in an open graph says false. A node without type: "object" (an anyOf wrapper) puts no constraint on keys; its members do. Multi-label vertices (see Multi-Label Vertices ): every label checks the properties it declares and its own required list; a top-level property that no label declares is allowed when ANY label admits additional properties (the same "any label" rule as topology). Coercion uses the first label, in label order, that declares the key. closed rejects a vertex without a label or with an undeclared label. Adding or removing a label re-validates the vertex under the new label set and commits only on success. Edge labels are single, but can be changed (set_label(..), GraphStorage::set_edge_label). The change checks the edge as stored under the new label (closed: a declared label and a declared connection; open and closed: the new label's required keys and declared types) and changes nothing on a violation. Stored values are not coerced by a label change (reads never coerce); later writes coerce by the new label's declarations. none describes without enforcing; the GraphML import still restores the declared logical types from it (uuid, the date and time types, array, object; see UUID Values ). A date or time is written to GraphML as its canonical text under a string key and read back as a temporal value where the target schema declares its format (text that is not of the type fails the import with InvalidAttributeValue); without a declaration it stays a string.
647.title: Modes and additionalProperties

648.body: An edge label declares its allowed connections ({"from": "Person", "to": "Company"}, * matches every label). Because labels are a set, an edge is accepted if ANY label of the source and ANY label of the target matches a declared connection. An edge label without connections allows every pair. A label change that would make an incident edge violate the connections is rejected as a whole.
648.title: Edge topology (closed)

649.body: The content of an object, array or anyOf value is validated at any depth: declared nested keys are type- and constraint-checked, required nested keys must be present, undeclared nested keys follow the object's additionalProperties. Errors name the canonical path ($.address.zip, $.items[1].n). A nested write (property(jpath("address.zip"), v)) coerces the leaf to the type declared at that location. See Path Keys (jpath) .
649.title: Nested values

65.body:
add_v, add_e, property and drop write. Every traversal is one unit: when any step fails, nothing it wrote stays. g.add_v("person").property("name", "ann").property("age", 41).as("a") .v().has("name", "marko").add_e("knows").to("a") .iterate();
g.v().has("name", "marko").out("knows").values("name") // ann, josh, vadas

651.body:
Seven methods, the same everywhere. They are plain calls on the graph source, not traversal steps (like g.statistics()); each runs in the current unit (a transaction, a whole-script unit) or as a unit of its own. Method Returns Authorization get_schema() the stored schema, or none (never inferred) Read on Schema set_schema(schema), set_schema(schema, mode) - (replaces the stored schema; mode replaces the schema's mode) Update on Schema patch_schema(patch) the new schema (JSON Merge Patch, RFC 7396, onto the stored one) Update on Schema validate_schema(schema), validate_schema(schema, mode) {violations, diff, compatible}: a dry run against the data Read on Schema validate_schema_patch(patch) the same for a patch Read on Schema infer_schema() the schema the data satisfies Read on Schema diff_schema(schema) {changes, compatible} from the stored schema Read on Schema Input Output Rust (GraphTraversalSource) GraphSchema (GraphSchema::from_json(text), from_value, or the builders), SchemaPatch (graphersal::schema) GraphSchema, SchemaValidation, SchemaDiff (to_value() gives the data shape) DSL (both spellings: get_schema/getSchema, ...) a map or JSON text a map Python (Graph.get_schema(), ...) a dict or JSON str (keyword policy=) a dict Playground engine (wasm getSchema, ...) JSON text JSON A map built in the DSL keeps its keys in alphabetical order (Rhai maps are sorted), so the property order of a schema that went through a map is alphabetical; JSON text and Python dicts keep it. The traversal step g.v()...infer_schema() infers over a stream, with the same inference. In a DSL map literal, quote the keys that are not plain identifiers: $ref, $defs, $schema and $id start with $. default (a word Rhai reserves) is accepted as a plain key in the Graphersal DSL, quoted or not: g.patch_schema(#{vertices: #{person: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{ age: #{type: ["integer", "null"], default: 7}
}}}}}) JSON text needs no quoting rules of its own: g.set_schema(text) takes the schema as written. A schema change is a database change : it advances the commit sequence number, makes the run mutated, is recorded as Mutation::SetSchema { before, after } (the canonical JSON) in the same change set as the data, rolls back with its unit, and is reported in the result's changes: {data, schema} (Execution::changes(), the DSL's r.changes, the playground's response). Validation is immediate: the existing data is checked when the schema is set, not at commit.
651.title: The schema methods

652.body: set_schema and patch_schema validate all existing data first , in one pass over the vertices and edges, when the mode is open or closed. If anything violates the schema, the graph and its current schema stay unchanged and the call fails with one aggregated error that lists every kind of violation, grouped by rule with a count and a few sample ids: Cannot apply the Closed schema: the existing data violates it (5 kinds of violations on 22 elements of 22 checked) 1) Person.age is declared mandatory but is missing on 12 vertices [ids: "p0", "p1", "p2", "p3", "p4" and 7 more] 2) vertex label Alien is not declared (Closed): 5 vertices [ids: "x0", "x1", "x2", "x3", "x4"] 3) Company.name is declared mandatory but is missing on 3 vertices [ids: "c0", "c1", "c2"] 4) Person.age has the wrong type on 1 vertex (declared int64, found string) [ids: "t"] 5) Robot.model is not declared (Closed) on 1 vertex [ids: "r"] A group is (kind, label, field or path): missing required keys, undeclared labels or properties, type mismatches, constraint violations, edge topology violations (closed) and nested path violations (Person $.address.zip is declared mandatory but is missing on 1 vertex). Every violation inside a value is listed, not only the first: all keys, all array items, at any depth, each under its own path ($.address.zip wrong type, $.address.street missing and $.address.city undeclared are three groups). Array indices are collapsed into [*]: a rule broken by any item of an array is ONE group ($.addresses[0].zip and $.addresses[2].zip missing are the group $.addresses[*].zip), which shows the first concrete path it met (Person $.addresses[*].zip is declared mandatory but is missing on 5 vertices (first at $.addresses[1].zip) [ids: ...]). Per node only the first failing constraint is named. An element counts once per group, however many of its items break the rule. A single write still fails on the first violation it meets. Groups are ordered by count (largest first), then kind, element, label and field, so the same data gives the same report. Each group shows its count and up to 5 sample ids (cut to 40 characters, escaped); at most 20 groups are printed, the structured report keeps up to 1000, further violations are only counted. Stored data is checked exactly as it is: nothing is coerced and nothing is written. validate_schema returns the same report as data: violations: {mode, elements_checked, violating_elements, total_violations, omitted_violations, groups: [{kind, element, label, field, example_field, detail, count, sample_ids, omitted_ids}]} (example_field is the first concrete path of a [*] field, null otherwise), with kind one of unknown_label, missing_required, type_mismatch, constraint_violation, undeclared_property, invalid_topology. How to proceed: fix or migrate the offending data, relax the schema (make a key optional, admit null, declare the label or property), apply it with mode none, or start from infer_schema(), which is valid for the data it came from.

652.title: Applying a schema to existing data

654.body: patch_schema applies a JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) to the canonical form of the stored schema ({} without one): an object merges member by member (property order is kept), null removes a member, any other value (an array too) replaces it. RFC 7396 cannot set a member to null; use set_schema for a "default": null. validate_schema_patch previews the result against the data. diff_schema lists the changes (kind, element, label, path such as $.address.zip or $.tags[*], before, after) and whether each is backward compatible : data and clients written against the old schema keep working: the old data stays valid and every write that followed the old schema still succeeds. In short, a compatible change only adds (an optional key, a label, an allowed value) or relaxes (a wider type, a looser bound, a less strict mode); tightening a rule or removing a declaration something could depend on (a label, a key of a closed object) is incompatible. This is the usual schema-registry convention: adding an optional property is compatible, also to an open object, and so is removing a property declaration from an open object (the key becomes an undeclared one, which the object admits; the change is still listed as property_removed). A server's "compatible changes only" policy can veto the rest in a before_commit hook. Change Compatible when mode it gets less strict (closed → open → none); open → closed is incompatible meta, annotations (title, description, ...) always default, defaultFunction (added, changed, removed; kind default_changed) always: it changes only what future creates store label added the old mode was closed (no client could write it), or its schema requires no key and admits undeclared keys (an open graph) label removed never connection added/removed the label's connections still allow every old pair (an empty list allows all), or the new mode is not closed (topology binds only there) property added it is optional (not in required), also in an open object property removed the object admits undeclared keys (open: mode open/none or additionalProperties: true), whether the key was optional or required; from a closed object never key made required / optional never / always additionalProperties false → true type the new type admits every kind the old one did ("integer" → ["integer", "null"]) minimum, maxLength, minItems, formatMinimum, ... removed or relaxed (a later formatMaximum, an earlier formatMinimum) format never (date → date-time is another type, so are adding and removing a format) pattern, const removed enum removed, or a superset A key the old schema listed in required without declaring it was written by every old client, with any value: declaring it later is compatible only if the declaration accepts everything. With a new mode none every change is compatible (nothing is enforced any more). The diff is static : it compares the two schemas, never the data. Existing data that conflicts with a compatible change (an element that already holds a newly declared optional key with another type, say) is found by validate_schema / validate_schema_patch, and set_schema refuses to apply the schema until it is fixed.
654.breadcrumbs: Schemas » Changing a schema: patch and diff

655.body: infer_schema() (and the step) report what the data holds, at every position: the kinds seen (a type array, or anyOf when a string, a uuid and the date and time types share a position: a datetime is {"type": "string", "format": "date-time"}), items of arrays, properties of objects, and required only for keys every object at that position has, at any depth (also inside arrays and next to other kinds). Every label of a vertex is declared; connections use the endpoints' first labels. The result has mode none and is valid for the data it came from in open and in closed mode (an unlabeled element has no label to declare, so closed rejects it; see Freeze the structure you have ). It never guesses from string content: a UUID-shaped string is a string. Inference statistics (counts) are not part of the format.
655.title: Inference

656.body: Format Shows table, markdown one row per property path (address.zip, roles[].name), type, required, nullable, constraints (0..150, length 1..80, pattern ^x$), notes (description, default, marked (annotation) where it is not applied: null or below the top level, defaultFunction) tree the labels and their properties as a tree json the canonical format jsonschema one standalone JSON Schema per label ($defs: vertex:person, edge:knows), the mode's default additionalProperties written out mermaid an erDiagram; nested objects are entities of their own (`person plantuml the label topology as entity diagrams, then a @startjson view of the condensed schema The meta-graph (schema.to_graph() in the DSL, GraphSchema::to_graph in Rust) has one vertex per vertex label and one edge per connection, each with its schema node as the schema property. The playground's Schema panel shows the same schema as editable tables, as JSON, as a graph of its labels (node size and count from the data) and as the Mermaid diagram, here for a small cloud inventory: The label graph of a schema: vertex labels with their counts, edge labels as arrows The Mermaid entity diagram of the same schema
656.title: Renderers

657.body: Model.model_json_schema() loads as a label schema as it is ($defs/$ref, anyOf with null, title, description, default, enum, const, exclusive*, additionalProperties: false, and the date and time fields: datetime ("format": "date-time"), date, time and timedelta ("format": "duration")), except for one thing to remove first: dict[str, T] fields ("additionalProperties": {..}): no map type; write {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": true}. A Pydantic time field is a time of day: Graphersal's time has no offset, so a text with one (10:00:00+02:00) is refused by the coercion (declare a date-time for an instant). Tuples (prefixItems) and Decimal (anyOf with a string pattern for some versions) are not supported either. The top level of the model must be an object ("type": "object"). A field's non-null default (active: bool = True) becomes a default on create in mode open/closed; the "default": null Pydantic writes on every optional field stores nothing.
657.title: Pasting a Pydantic model

658.body: The schema is validated per storage call (one add_v with its folded properties, one single property(key, value), one drop, ...), and every traversal is one unit of work: when a call fails, the whole traversal is rolled back, including what its earlier steps wrote (see Transactions ). In the playground a refused write shows the failing step and how to fix it (here a closed schema that declares cpus as int64): A schema violation in the Results panel with its help text Case Test property(map) with several entries schema_gap_tests::gap4_property_map_is_atomic property_json (Rust API) schema_gap_tests::gap4_property_json_is_atomic mergeV/mergeE option(Merge.onMatch, map) with several entries schema_gap_tests::gap4_merge_v_on_match_is_atomic addE over several start vertices schema_gap_tests::gap4_add_e_over_several_endpoints_is_atomic any traversal with several steps transaction_tests::a_schema_violation_rolls_back_the_whole_traversal A GraphML import into an existing graph is one unit too: an invalid element rolls back the elements imported before it. GraphML carries no schema: set the schema first, then import. The CLI does both in that order with graphersal --graph g.graphml --schema schema.json [--schema-mode closed] (also for GraphSON, and with --server); a violation stops the start with exit code 1.

659.body:
A saved query is a named, parameterized piece of DSL stored IN the database, next to the schema: written once, called by name from any front end (the CLI, Python, the playground). g.query("older_than", #{age: 30}).values("name").toList()
// ["josh", "peter"] The body is the text of ONE Rhai function; its parameters are named and typed. A call returns what the function returns: a traversal can be continued by the caller (like a SQL view), a value (a number, a list, a map) is a value (like a stored procedure). Saved queries are read-only, always : a query never writes data, the schema, the saved queries or files, not even through a query it calls or a traversal it returns. Queries live in folders (an attribute, not part of the name) and carry an optional description . Every example on this page was run with graphersal on the default modern graph; the line after // is its real output. Each block starts from a fresh graph.
659.title: Saved Queries

669.body: The catalog is part of the database: a Store keeps it in its snapshots and journal, losslessly (every catalog change is a durable commit; recovery, rollback, forks and backups carry it), and a packed snapshot (.gsnap) carries it too. A query is stored as its source text, never as a compiled plan: every call plans anew. GraphML and GraphSON carry no saved queries, like they carry no schema. The byte layout is in the format spec (sections 6.3, 9.3 and 16).
